title: Scalar and vector products
summary: There are two ways to multiply [[vector|vectors]]. The [[scalar-product|scalar product]] $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$ gives a number, which finds angles and tests for right angles. The [[vector-product|vector product]] $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ gives a vector at right angles to both, and its length is an area. Together they split a wind or a force into the part along a direction and the part across it.

goals.text: Calculate a [[scalar-product|scalar product]] from components and say what it means in context, such as a total cost.
Find the angle between two vectors and the acute angle between two lines, and use $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w} = 0$ to test whether non-zero vectors are perpendicular.
Calculate a [[vector-product|vector product]], check it is perpendicular to both vectors, and use the right-hand screw rule for its direction, with no proofs needed.
Find the area of a parallelogram or a triangle from $\lvert\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}\rvert$.
Find the [[component-of-a-vector-in-a-direction|component of a vector in a direction]] and at right angles to it, and interpret each in context.

synonyms: area of a triangle using vectors
component of a vector in a direction

before.hint: Square each component, add, then take the square root.

before.prompt: A is $(2, 5, -1)$ and B is $(6, 3, 4)$. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
before.hint: Start at A and finish at B: subtract A's coordinates from B's.

before.prompt: Which vector is a [[direction-vector|direction vector]] of the line $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\4\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-5\\3\end{pmatrix}$?
before.hint: The direction is the vector multiplied by the parameter, or any non-zero multiple of it.
before.explain: $\begin{pmatrix}-4\\10\\-6\end{pmatrix} = -2\begin{pmatrix}2\\-5\\3\end{pmatrix}$, a multiple of the vector beside $\lambda$. The vector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\4\end{pmatrix}$ is a point on the line, not its direction. Revise it in {{lesson:3.11}}.

blocks.text: In {{lesson:3.10}} you added vectors and scaled them. The [[scalar-product|scalar product]] multiplies two vectors: multiply matching [[component-of-a-vector|components]], then add.
For example, $\begin{pmatrix}3\\2\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix}5\\-4\end{pmatrix} = 15 - 8 = 7$. The answer is one number, a scalar, which gives the product its name.

blocks.statement: The scalar product of $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ is the number $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$ found by multiplying their matching components and adding the results.
blocks.plain: Read it as v dot w. Many books call it the dot product.

blocks.text: This is in the booklet. In 2D, leave out the third product. Order doesn't matter: $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w} = \boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{v}$. In context it often adds up a total, such as a total cost.

blocks.question: Find $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$ for $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\-2\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: Multiply matching components, keeping the signs: $4 \times 2 = 8$, $(-1) \times 5 = -5$ and $3 \times (-2) = -6$.
Add: $8 - 5 - 6 = -3$. A scalar product can be negative, and it has no components.

blocks.question: A café orders $12$ kg of coffee, $30$ kg of sugar and $8$ kg of cocoa, so $\boldsymbol{q} = \begin{pmatrix}12\\30\\8\end{pmatrix}$. The prices per kilogram, in dollars, are $\boldsymbol{p} = \begin{pmatrix}14.50\\1.20\\9.75\end{pmatrix}$. Find $\boldsymbol{q} \cdot \boldsymbol{p}$ and interpret it.
steps: Multiply matching components: $12 \times 14.50 = 174$, $30 \times 1.20 = 36$ and $8 \times 9.75 = 78$. Each is kilograms times dollars per kilogram, the cost of one item.
Add: $174 + 36 + 78 = 288$. So $\boldsymbol{q} \cdot \boldsymbol{p}$ is the total cost of the order, $288.00$ dollars.

blocks.hint: The coefficients of $\boldsymbol{i}$, $\boldsymbol{j}$ and $\boldsymbol{k}$ are the components. Watch the signs.

blocks.prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with force $\boldsymbol{F} = \begin{pmatrix}25\\-10\\40\end{pmatrix}$ N through displacement $\boldsymbol{s} = \begin{pmatrix}6\\3\\0.5\end{pmatrix}$ m. The work done, in joules, is $\boldsymbol{F} \cdot \boldsymbol{s}$. Find it.

blocks.text: The [[scalar-product|scalar product]] also measures how much two vectors point the same way. The angle $\theta$ between $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ is measured with both drawn from the same point, and lies from $0^{\circ}$ to $180^{\circ}$.

blocks.tex: \boldsymbol{v}\cdot\boldsymbol{w} = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\cos\theta, \text{ where } \theta \text{ is the angle between } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w}

blocks.text: Rearranged for $\cos\theta$, it finds an angle:

Both are in the booklet. The magnitudes are positive, so the sign of $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w}$ gives the type of angle: positive is acute, zero is a right angle, negative is obtuse. Drag the tips below and watch the sign change at $90^{\circ}$.

blocks.alt: Two vectors a and b drawn from the origin on a grid, with an arc marking the angle between them. Dragging either tip updates the scalar product, both magnitudes, cos theta and the angle in degrees. When the scalar product is zero, a right-angle mark appears and the vectors are reported as perpendicular.

blocks.question: Two guy ropes run from the top T of a tent pole to pegs A and B. In metres, $\overrightarrow{TA} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\-2\\-6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{TB} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\-8\end{pmatrix}$. Find the angle between the ropes, to 1 d.p.
steps: Both vectors start at T. Scalar product: $-3 - 8 + 48 = 37$, which is positive, so expect an acute angle.
Magnitudes: $\sqrt{9 + 4 + 36} = 7$ and $\sqrt{1 + 16 + 64} = 9$. These are the rope lengths in metres.
$\cos\theta = \frac{37}{7 \times 9} = \frac{37}{63}$, so in degree mode $\theta = 54.034\ldots^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: For an angle at a corner of a triangle, use two vectors that both leave that corner. For the angle at A, use $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

blocks.question: A surveyor stands at $\mathrm{A}(2, 1, 0)$ and sights two marker poles at $\mathrm{B}(10, 7, 3)$ and $\mathrm{C}(-4, 9, 5)$, in metres. Use your calculator to find angle BAC, to 1 d.p.
steps: Both vectors must leave A: $\overrightarrow{AB} = \begin{pmatrix}8\\6\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC} = \begin{pmatrix}-6\\8\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
Scalar product: $-48 + 48 + 15 = 15$. Magnitudes: $\sqrt{109}$ and $\sqrt{125}$.
Write the expression down: $\cos\theta = \frac{15}{\sqrt{109}\sqrt{125}}$. This line earns the method mark.
Type $\cos^{-1}$ of it in one line, in degree mode: $\theta = 82.616\ldots^{\circ}$. Round only now. The poles are close to, but not at, a right angle as seen from A.

blocks.text: Using the position vectors $\boldsymbol{b}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ for angle BAC. They start at the origin, not at A. Find $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ first.

blocks.statement: For non-zero vectors, $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w} = 0$ exactly when $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ are perpendicular.
blocks.why: $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert$ are not zero, so $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\cos\theta = 0$ only when $\cos\theta = 0$, which means $\theta = 90^{\circ}$.

blocks.prompt: In a frame design, a strut has direction $\begin{pmatrix}3\\k\\-1\end{pmatrix}$ and must be perpendicular to a beam with direction $\begin{pmatrix}k\\-2\\5\end{pmatrix}$. Find $k$.
blocks.hint: Set the scalar product equal to $0$. The unknown appears in two of the products.

blocks.text: A line's [[direction-vector|direction vector]] can point either way along it, so two lines make angles $\theta$ and $180^{\circ} - \theta$. The angle between the lines is the acute one. Find the angle between the direction vectors, and if it is obtuse, subtract it from $180^{\circ}$.

blocks.question: Two straight tunnels are modelled by the lines $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\-20\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}10\\5\\-20\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Find the acute angle between the tunnels, to 1 d.p.
steps: Use only the direction vectors $\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-3\\6\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Scalar product: $-6 - 6 + 4 = -8$. Magnitudes: $3$ and $7$.
$\cos\theta = -\frac{8}{21}$, so $\theta = 112.39\ldots^{\circ}$, obtuse because the scalar product is negative.
The acute angle is $180^{\circ} - 112.39\ldots^{\circ} = 67.607\ldots^{\circ}$: the tunnels' directions cross at about $67.6^{\circ}$.

blocks.prompt: Find the acute angle between the lines $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\0\end{pmatrix} + \lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{r} = \begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\7\end{pmatrix} + \mu\begin{pmatrix}6\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$. Give your answer in degrees, to 1 d.p.
blocks.hint: Use the direction vectors only. If the angle is obtuse, subtract it from 180 degrees.
blocks.explain: Scalar product $6 - 4 - 6 = -4$, magnitudes $3$ and $7$. So $\cos\theta = -\frac{4}{21}$ and $\theta = 100.98\ldots^{\circ}$. The acute angle is $180^{\circ} - 100.98\ldots^{\circ} \approx 79.0^{\circ}$.

blocks.text: Sometimes you need a direction at right angles to two vectors, such as the way a solar panel faces. The [[vector-product|vector product]] gives it. Two non-parallel vectors from one point lie in a plane, and a rule picks one of the two directions perpendicular to it.

blocks.statement: For two vectors with angle $\theta$ between them, $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ is the vector of length $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$ along $\boldsymbol{n}$, a [[unit-vector|unit vector]] at right angles to both $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$. The right-hand screw rule fixes which of the two perpendicular directions $\boldsymbol{n}$ takes.
blocks.plain: Read it as v cross w. Many books call it the cross product.

blocks.text: The right-hand screw rule: point the fingers of your right hand along $\boldsymbol{v}$ and curl them towards $\boldsymbol{w}$. Your thumb points along $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$, the way a screw moves when turned from $\boldsymbol{v}$ to $\boldsymbol{w}$.

blocks.alt: Vectors v and w are drawn from the same point in a flat shaded plane, with the angle theta between them and a curved arrow turning from v towards w. The vector v cross w points straight up out of the plane. A dashed vector w cross v points straight down, the opposite way.
blocks.caption: Turning from $\boldsymbol{v}$ to $\boldsymbol{w}$ sends $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ up. Turning the other way sends $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v}$ down.

blocks.text: Swap the order and you curl the other way: $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v} = -(\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w})$. In practice you use this booklet formula. It needs 3D vectors, so give a 2D vector a third component of $0$.
You won't be asked to prove anything about either product. Use them as tools, and check each vector product: its scalar product with both vectors must be $0$.

blocks.question: Find $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$ for $\boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}$.
steps: First component: $v_{2}w_{3} - v_{3}w_{2} = 1 \times 4 - (-3) \times (-2) = 4 - 6 = -2$.
Second component: $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3} = (-3) \times 1 - 2 \times 4 = -3 - 8 = -11$.
Third component: $v_{1}w_{2} - v_{2}w_{1} = 2 \times (-2) - 1 \times 1 = -4 - 1 = -5$.
Check: with $\boldsymbol{v}$, $-4 - 11 + 15 = 0$, and with $\boldsymbol{w}$, $-2 + 22 - 20 = 0$. The answer is perpendicular to both.

blocks.question: A flat solar panel has its lowest corner at the origin, with $z$ pointing up. One edge runs along $\boldsymbol{p} = \begin{pmatrix}5\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and the other up the roof along $\boldsymbol{q} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\4\\2.5\end{pmatrix}$, in metres. (a) Find $\boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{q}$. (b) Does it point up, away from the roof, or down into it? What about $\boldsymbol{q} \times \boldsymbol{p}$?
steps: Check: the scalar products with $\boldsymbol{p}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}$ are $12.5 - 12.5 + 0 = 0$ and $-2.5 - 50 + 52.5 = 0$. It is perpendicular to the panel.
(b) The $z$-component, $21$, is positive, so $\boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{q}$ points up, away from the roof.
$\boldsymbol{q} \times \boldsymbol{p} = -(\boldsymbol{p} \times \boldsymbol{q})$ lies along the same line but points down into the roof.

blocks.text: Getting the sign of the middle component wrong. It is $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$. The two scalar-product checks catch this slip, so always do them.

blocks.hint: Use the booklet formula one component at a time, then check your answer against both vectors.
blocks.explain: $0(1) - (-3)(4) = 12$, $(-3)(2) - 1(1) = -7$ and $1(4) - 0(2) = 4$. The wrong options come from a middle-sign slip, the reversed order, and multiplying matching components.

blocks.text: When you know two lengths and the angle, but not the components, use the booklet formula for the length:

blocks.tex: \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta, \text{ where } \theta \text{ is the angle between } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w}

blocks.prompt: $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert = 6$, $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert = 3.5$ and the angle between $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$ is $40^{\circ}$. Find $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$, correct to 3 significant figures.
blocks.hint: Use $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$, with your GDC in degree mode.

blocks.text: Draw a parallelogram with adjacent sides $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$, angle $\theta$ between them, and $\boldsymbol{v}$ as the base.

blocks.alt: A parallelogram with base v along the bottom and side w leaving the same corner at angle theta. A dashed vertical height of length w sin theta drops from the top of w to the base, meeting it at a right angle. A diagonal from the end of v to the end of w cuts off a shaded triangle with sides v and w.
blocks.caption: The height is $\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$. The shaded triangle is half the parallelogram.

blocks.text: Base times height (prior learning in the booklet) gives $\lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta$, which is exactly $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$.

blocks.tex: A = \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram}

blocks.text: A diagonal cuts the parallelogram into two equal triangles, so a triangle has half the area:

blocks.tex: A = \frac{1}{2}\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ are two sides of a triangle from the same vertex}

blocks.text: For triangle PQR, use two sides leaving one corner, such as $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR}$, never the corners' position vectors.

blocks.question: A parallelogram-shaped skylight has adjacent edges $\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ m and $\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ m. Find its area, to 3 s.f.
steps: Vector product: $\begin{pmatrix}1 \times 2 - 0 \times 2\\0 \times 1 - 3 \times 2\\3 \times 2 - 1 \times 1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-6\\5\end{pmatrix}$.
Its length is the area: $\sqrt{4 + 36 + 25} = \sqrt{65} = 8.0622\ldots$ square metres. $\sqrt{65}$ is the exact value.

blocks.question: A triangular shade sail is fixed at $\mathrm{P}(0, 0, 2.5)$, $\mathrm{Q}(4.2, 0.6, 3.1)$ and $\mathrm{R}(1.5, 3.8, 2.2)$, in metres. The fabric costs $18.50$ dollars per square metre. Use your calculator to find the cost of the fabric for the sail.
steps: Two sides leaving P: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix}4.2\\0.6\\0.6\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}1.5\\3.8\\-0.3\end{pmatrix}$.
Vector product: $\overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR} = \begin{pmatrix}-2.46\\2.16\\15.06\end{pmatrix}$.
Cost: $18.50 \times 7.7058\ldots = 142.558\ldots$ dollars, rounded only now. Rounding the area to $7.71$ first gives $142.64$, which is wrong.

blocks.text: Forgetting the $\frac{1}{2}$ for a triangle, or putting it in for a parallelogram. $\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert$ is the parallelogram, and the triangle is half of it.

blocks.prompt: A triangular flower bed on a slope has corners $\mathrm{K}(1, 0, 2)$, $\mathrm{L}(4, 2, 2)$ and $\mathrm{M}(0, 5, 3)$, in metres. Find its area.
blocks.hint: Use $\overrightarrow{KL}$ and $\overrightarrow{KM}$, both leaving K. Then halve the length of their vector product.
blocks.explain: $\overrightarrow{KL} \times \overrightarrow{KM} = \begin{pmatrix}3\\2\\0\end{pmatrix} \times \begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\1\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\17\end{pmatrix}$, with length $\sqrt{302} = 17.37\ldots$. Half is $8.69$ m$^{2}$. $17.4$ forgets the half, and $3.74$ uses the position vectors of K and L.

blocks.prompt: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram-shaped field are $\boldsymbol{u}$ and $\boldsymbol{v}$, in metres, and $\boldsymbol{u} \times \boldsymbol{v} = \begin{pmatrix}40\\-30\\120\end{pmatrix}$. Find the area of the field, in square metres.
blocks.hint: The area is the length of the vector product, not the vector itself.

sections.heading: Components along and across a direction

blocks.text: A pilot taking off cares about two parts of the wind: the part along the runway and the part pushing sideways across it. So you often split a vector $\boldsymbol{a}$ into a part along a direction $\boldsymbol{b}$ and a part at right angles to it.

blocks.alt: Vector a and vector b start from the same point O with the angle theta between them, b lying along a horizontal line. A dashed line drops from the tip of a to the line of b, meeting it at a right angle at F. The segment from O to F along b is labelled a dot b over the length of b, equal to the length of a times cos theta. The dashed perpendicular from the tip of a to F is labelled the length of a cross b over the length of b, equal to the length of a times sin theta.
blocks.caption: Along $\boldsymbol{b}$: $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\cos\theta$. Across $\boldsymbol{b}$, in the plane of the two vectors: $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\sin\theta$.

blocks.text: The right-angled triangle gives $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\cos\theta$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\sin\theta$. Divide the two product formulas by $\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert$ to get these from components.

blocks.term: Component of a vector in a direction
blocks.statement: For a non-zero vector $\boldsymbol{b}$, the component of $\boldsymbol{a}$ in the direction of $\boldsymbol{b}$ is the scalar $\frac{\boldsymbol{a} \cdot \boldsymbol{b}}{\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert} = \lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\cos\theta$. The component of $\boldsymbol{a}$ perpendicular to $\boldsymbol{b}$, in the plane of the two vectors, is $\frac{\lvert \boldsymbol{a} \times \boldsymbol{b} \rvert}{\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert} = \lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\sin\theta$.
blocks.plain: How much of a points along b, and how much points straight across it.

blocks.text: Learn these: they are not in the booklet. The component along $\boldsymbol{b}$ is negative when $\theta > 90^{\circ}$, meaning that part of $\boldsymbol{a}$ points against $\boldsymbol{b}$. The perpendicular component is a length, so it is never negative.

blocks.question: A plane takes off in the direction $\boldsymbol{d} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}$, with $x$ east, $y$ north and $z$ up. The wind velocity is $\boldsymbol{w} = \begin{pmatrix}-15\\8\\0\end{pmatrix}$ km h$^{-1}$. Find the component of the wind in the direction of take-off, and interpret it.
steps: $\boldsymbol{w} \cdot \boldsymbol{d} = -60 + 24 + 0 = -36$ and $\lvert\boldsymbol{d}\rvert = \sqrt{16 + 9} = 5$.
Component along $\boldsymbol{d}$: $\frac{-36}{5} = -7.2$ km h$^{-1}$.
Interpret: it is negative, so this part of the wind blows against the plane, a headwind of $7.2$ km h$^{-1}$.

check.prompt: Now find the crosswind: the component of $\boldsymbol{w}$ perpendicular to $\boldsymbol{d}$, in km h$^{-1}$.
check.hint: Take the length of $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{d}$, then divide by $\lvert\boldsymbol{d}\rvert = 5$.
check.explain: $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{d} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\-45 - 32\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\-77\end{pmatrix}$, so the crosswind is $\frac{77}{5} = 15.4$ km h$^{-1}$. Check: $7.2^{2} + 15.4^{2} = 289 = \lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert^{2}$.

blocks.question: A winch cable pulls a cart up a straight ramp with force $\boldsymbol{F} = \begin{pmatrix}40\\25\\30\end{pmatrix}$ N. The ramp runs in the direction $\boldsymbol{d} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\0.5\end{pmatrix}$. Use your calculator to find (a) the component of $\boldsymbol{F}$ along the ramp and (b) the component perpendicular to the ramp, in the plane of $\boldsymbol{F}$ and $\boldsymbol{d}$. Give answers to 3 s.f.
steps: $\lvert\boldsymbol{d}\rvert = \sqrt{4 + 1 + 0.25} = \sqrt{5.25}$.
(a) $\boldsymbol{F} \cdot \boldsymbol{d} = 80 + 25 + 15 = 120$, so along the ramp: $\frac{120}{\sqrt{5.25}} = 52.372\ldots \approx 52.4$ N. This part pulls the cart up the ramp.

(b) $\boldsymbol{F} \times \boldsymbol{d} = \begin{pmatrix}-17.5\\40\\-10\end{pmatrix}$, so perpendicular: $\frac{\sqrt{2006.25}}{\sqrt{5.25}} = 19.548\ldots \approx 19.5$ N. This part doesn't move the cart along the ramp.
Check: $52.372\ldots^{2} + 19.548\ldots^{2} = 3125 = \lvert\boldsymbol{F}\rvert^{2}$.
blocks.answer: (a) $\approx 52.4\text{ N}$ along the ramp; (b) $\text{perpendicular component} \approx 19.5\text{ N}$

blocks.text: Dividing by the wrong length. The component of $\boldsymbol{a}$ along $\boldsymbol{b}$ divides by $\lvert\boldsymbol{b}\rvert$, the direction you are measuring along, not by $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert$.

blocks.prompt: A drone flies with velocity $\begin{pmatrix}6\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}$ m s$^{-1}$. Find the component of its velocity in the direction $\begin{pmatrix}2\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}$, in m s$^{-1}$.
blocks.hint: Find the scalar product, then divide by the length of the direction vector.
blocks.explain: $\frac{12 - 4 + 3}{\sqrt{4 + 4 + 1}} = \frac{11}{3}$ m s$^{-1}$. $\frac{11}{7}$ divides by the drone's speed, and $\frac{11}{9}$ by the length squared.

blocks.prompt: A force of $20$ N acts at $35^{\circ}$ to the direction a box can slide. Find the component of the force in that direction, to 3 s.f.
blocks.hint: You know the magnitude and the angle, so use $\lvert\boldsymbol{a}\rvert\cos\theta$.

blocks.text: For non-zero vectors, $\boldsymbol{v} \cdot \boldsymbol{w} = 0$ exactly when they are perpendicular. A positive scalar product means an acute angle, and a negative one means an obtuse angle.
The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors, taken as acute or right: if you get $\theta > 90^{\circ}$, use $180^{\circ} - \theta$.

$\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} = \lvert\boldsymbol{v}\rvert\lvert\boldsymbol{w}\rvert\sin\theta\,\boldsymbol{n}$ with $\theta$ the angle between $\boldsymbol{v}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}$. It is perpendicular to both, since $\boldsymbol{n}$ is a unit vector at right angles to each, pointing the way the right-hand screw rule gives. Order matters: $\boldsymbol{w} \times \boldsymbol{v} = -(\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w})$.

blocks.tex: A = \lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ form two adjacent sides of a parallelogram}
A = \frac{1}{2}\lvert \boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w} \rvert, \text{ where } \boldsymbol{v} \text{ and } \boldsymbol{w} \text{ are two sides of a triangle from the same vertex}

mistakes: Using position vectors for an angle or an area. First find sides that leave the same corner, such as $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$.
Giving an obtuse angle between two lines. That angle is never obtuse, so use $180^{\circ} - \theta$ if $\theta > 90^{\circ}$.
A sign slip in the middle entry of $\boldsymbol{v} \times \boldsymbol{w}$, which is $v_{3}w_{1} - v_{1}w_{3}$. Check that your answer has a scalar product of $0$ with both vectors.
Missing out the $\frac{1}{2}$ for a triangle, or putting it in for a parallelogram.
Rounding $\cos\theta$, an area or a component before the last step. Keep the calculator's full value.
Finding an angle in radian mode when the question wants degrees. Check the mode before you use $\cos^{-1}$.
examTips: “Find” an angle: write $\cos\theta$ with your numbers substituted before giving the angle. That line earns the method mark, and a wrong value used correctly later can still earn follow-through marks.
“Show that” two vectors are perpendicular: show the scalar product is $0$ and say “so the vectors are perpendicular”. A bare “$90^{\circ}$” earns nothing.
“Find” an area: show the vector product's components, then its length. Write the expression you enter and give the area to 3 s.f., in square units.
“Interpret” a component: say what it means in context, with its unit. A negative component along a direction points against it, such as a headwind.
